synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, 17 Apr – 1 May 2026
synthesis.summary: In the two weeks following the Iran ceasefire, four reinforcing cracks are visible. (1) Command vacuum: Ali Khamenei was killed on 28 Feb; nominal successor Mojtaba is reportedly injured and absent, with the IRGC running wartime decisions through a generals' 'board' — even as the leader's office insists Mojtaba is in full health. (2) Currency collapse: the rial fell to a record ~1.8M/USD on 29 Apr (down >10% in a week post-ceasefire), with bread and medicine becoming visibly scarcer. (3) Labor unrest re-ignites: despite a martial-law atmosphere and a months-long internet blackout, steel pensioners, Karnameh-Sabz teachers, railway technicians, and refinery workers held simultaneous rallies in Esfahan/Tehran/Shush/Andimeshk. The truckers' guild appears to have been bought off (fuel-advance paid 22 Apr). (4) Infrastructure & repression squeeze: ≥59-day internet blackout costing >$1.8B, Tehran water at the brink (Pezeshkian flagging 500,000 toman/m³ Persian-Gulf transfer cost), school silent-strike entering weeks, and execution sentences for protesters (Tabari 1 May, Azadvar reportedly 30 Apr). The brittle equilibrium is held by IRGC coercion, an emergency information clamp, and a regime hope that talks with the U.S. produce sanctions relief before the rial / streets break.
synthesis.limitations: Window is two weeks, post-ceasefire. Deep on-the-ground signal is dampened by Iran's national internet blackout, which forces reliance on diaspora amplifiers and Persian-language outlets in exile (Kayhan London, Independent Persian, VOA Persian, Euronews Persian, HRANA). Counts of dead/arrested/striking carry significant uncertainty.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v2 — adding clergy, students, prisons, pharma, cyber (17 Apr – 1 May 2026)
synthesis.summary: Six new cracks crystallise alongside the four previously documented cracks. (5) Clerical defection: Mowlawi Abdolhamid — Iran's most-followed Sunni Friday-prayer leader — said publicly on 21 Apr that the country's air defence is broken and that the only path is a 'fair agreement' plus 'accountability for extremists who brought the country to ruin'. The regime answered by sealing the Makki Mosque-affiliated Azizi institute and freezing his associates' bank accounts. Former president Hassan Rouhani separately demanded a 'great change' and openly mocked attempts to grant '1% of demands while forgetting 99%' — an establishment-pragmatist break that contradicts the IRGC line. (6) Student strikes: Sharif University of Technology students started a class boycott from 25 Apr over the continued detention of Parnian Khodabakhshi; Beheshti University and others showed parallel disciplinary tension. (7) Prison resistance escalating: 'Tuesdays of No to Executions' hunger strike entered its 117th, then 118th week across 56 prisons, with female inmates joining despite explicit threats; 7 political prisoners were violently transferred from Evin to Qezel-Hesar Ward 3, which an Iran HRS exposé described as a 'silent execution chamber'. (8) Pharma collapse: drug prices up to 380% above pre-war levels; Persian financial press warning of a generalised drug crisis within two months; the parliament Health Commission's spokesperson explicitly warned of an imminent morphine shortage. (9) Cyber pressure on the bank-IRGC link: hackers claiming Israeli alignment said they destroyed data inside the IRGC-affiliated Bank Sepah, while Iran's Central Bank publicly denied 'the banking network surrendered'. (10) Kurdish escalation: a new wave of mass arrests across Kurdish-majority cities, with Western analysts (Jamestown) openly war-gaming a Kurdish capture of territory. Together with the four prior cracks (command vacuum, currency collapse, labour unrest, infrastructure & repression squeeze), the regime now faces simultaneous pressure on its religious legitimacy, its medical capacity, its banking integrity, and three large ethnic frontiers (Baluchistan, Kurdistan, Tehran-bourgeois students) — while official-mouthpiece denials about Mojtaba's health and the central bank's invulnerability are themselves diagnostic of strain.
synthesis.limitations: Iran's national internet blackout still distorts on-the-ground signal. Hostile-source bias is mitigated by privileging Persian-language outlets and by recording regime denials alongside opposition reports. Casualty and prisoner counts retain wide error bars.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v3 — everyday scarcity, water rationing, memory repression
synthesis.summary: The newer Persian-source layer shifts the crack map from elite and security stress into ordinary daily life. Bread is no longer just inflation: citizen reports describe flour shortages, long bakery lines, and bread prices far above official rates, while an MP admits neither citizens nor bakers are satisfied with bread management despite a 504-hemmat subsidy. Tehran is already under de facto nightly water restriction, with overnight pressure reductions across neighborhoods to preserve reservoirs. Staple foods are pricing out households: eggs doubled over three weeks, macaroni jumped 31%, chicken is above start-of-year levels, and lamb is around 1.9-2.2 million toman/kg. Healthcare pressure is now visible at the level of a simple cold costing roughly 2 million toman, while cancer drug cycles can reach hundreds of millions. Repression is also moving into memory control: protest-dead graves in Rasht and Tehran are reportedly being cemented over, broken, or forced to remove dissident wording. HRANA's May Day report shows labor action has not disappeared under wartime pressure: hundreds of labor/guild gatherings and strikes continued over the previous year alongside arrests, lashes, prison sentences, fines, and exile terms. Kurdish detention pressure continues with named arrests in Naqadeh and Sardasht. The synthesis is therefore no longer just command vacuum plus currency collapse; it is command vacuum, currency collapse, labor unrest, water stress, medicine stress, bread/food stress, and memory-policing all arriving together.
synthesis.limitations: This pass favors Persian media and near-ground reports from the last two weeks; several high-value claims are still single-outlet or citizen-report based. xPool searches for current Farsi X terms returned no useful current items in this pass, likely a data-access/search-window limitation rather than absence of ground chatter.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v4 — digital class split, wage pressure, execution tempo, war-damaged infrastructure
synthesis.summary: The fourth pass adds four crack-planes to the v3 everyday-scarcity picture. First, the internet blackout has produced a visible class split: 'Internet Pro' is now criticized by citizens as rent/betrayal and by the judiciary chief as discrimination and corruption, with reports of large payments and operator overcharging. Second, repression is accelerating through named protester executions: HRANA's Sasan Azadvar file describes a 21-year-old protest detainee executed within days of Supreme Court confirmation, with alleged legal contradictions, forced-confession concerns, and security-restricted burial. Third, livelihood protests are spreading across wage-dependent institutions: university employees, health workers, drivers/claimants, steel retirees, and teachers all appear in late-April/May reports, while the Social Security debt and delayed salaries are becoming political facts. Fourth, war damage is now measurable in the production and grid layer: about 90 factories in Saveh/Arak reportedly faced shutdown/layoff pressure, Darugar workers had 3-5 months wage arrears, and officials acknowledged 2,000 serious electricity-network damages even while claiming rapid restoration. The regime is still functioning, but the stress field is broadening: command/succession opacity, currency collapse, bread-food-medicine scarcity, water pressure cuts, internet tiering, execution tempo, labor arrears, and infrastructure damage are no longer separate stories.
synthesis.limitations: This pass still privileges Persian media and rights/labor reporting, which is appropriate for near-ground signal but leaves regime-confirmed counter-narratives uneven except where official statements are embedded in the reports. Hijab-policing results were excluded because the strongest hit was an older republished item, not a clean current artifact.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v5 — professional refusal and quantified household squeeze
synthesis.summary: The fifth pass sharpens two v4 themes. synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v7 — health access becomes institutional grievance
synthesis.summary: The seventh pass strengthens v6's health-access thesis. The medicine crisis is no longer only item-level price shock or pharmacy scarcity: Iran's Rare Diseases Foundation warned insurers that vague definitions can deprive patients of support, and its head said even a short drug interruption can disrupt rare-disease treatment. Steel retirees in Isfahan and Tehran add a protest-side version of the same pressure, with ILNA directly reporting nine days without supplementary insurance and severe treatment, medicine, equipment, and hospital costs. The May Day wage picture adds household context: the 1405 minimum wage rose nominally but fell from about $125 to about $90 in one year, while official inflation and labor basket estimates show basic living costs far beyond minimum pay. xPool found no corroborating recent Tehran water posts, so the water-cut item remains only low-confidence texture. Net: the strongest current crack map clusters around treatment continuity, insurance coverage, medicine costs, and purchasing-power collapse rather than a single isolated protest sector.
synthesis.limitations: The rare-disease evidence is institutional and medical-warning evidence, not yet direct patient mobilization. The wage-dollar comparison depends on open-market exchange-rate assumptions. The xPool Tehran water query returned no recent corroborating posts, so water remains low confidence until service notices or multiple local reports appear.

information_depth.rationale: v7 combines direct Persian health-institution sources, a direct labor-source protest report already in the ledger, and a May Day wage/inflation article with concrete figures.

change.reason: v7 adds rare-disease insurance/medicine-continuity evidence, direct ILNA health-cost detail for steel retirees, and May Day wage-purchasing-power measurement.

claim.statement: On 29 April 2026, ILNA published direct accounts from low-income workers and retirees in Tehran, Rasht, and Sanandaj showing treatment triage: a service worker said metformin rose from 170,000 to 450,000-500,000 toman and she paid 13 million toman upfront for several months of medicine despite a 20 million toman salary and 10 million toman rent; a retired heart patient said he could not afford Plavix and stretched specialist visits; and a private-school teacher with thyroid cancer said each two-week prescription rose from 300,000 to 900,000 toman while tests cost 3 million every 45 days and insurance paid about 10%.
claim.subject: Iranian low-income workers and retirees with chronic illness
claim.object: medicine rationing, skipped care, and large out-of-pocket payments

evidence.summary: ILNA reported named worker/retiree cases from Tehran, Rasht, and Sanandaj, with medication price jumps, skipped Plavix, delayed specialist visits, 13M upfront medicine spending, and insurance covering only about 10% of some test costs.

information_depth.rationale: Direct Persian labor-source reporting includes city, condition, medication names, income, rent, price changes, and insurance details.

claim.statement: On 20 April 2026, ILNA reported that Salman Eshaghi, spokesman for parliament's Health and Treatment Commission, said the commission had reviewed price increases for some medicines caused by coordination failures among agencies; he acknowledged that in some cases patients' payment shares had risen and caused dissatisfaction, while claiming subsequent insurance-system corrections had improved the situation and that hard-to-treat disease medicines were covered at 90-95%.
claim.subject: Iran parliament health commission
claim.object: drug price and patient co-pay disruptions

evidence.summary: ILNA quoted Salman Eshaghi describing committee review of medicine price rises, patient co-pay increases, insurance correction measures, and claimed 90-95% coverage for hard-to-treat disease medicines.

information_depth.rationale: The official statement confirms administrative disruption and patient-payment effects but the claimed fixes need independent verification.

assessment.uncertainty: Government claims that corrections largely resolved the issue are not independently verified by the same source.

claim.statement: On 19 April 2026, Iran International reported Saeed Fatahi of the Supreme Center of Iranian Workers' Guild Associations warning that treatment and drug costs had risen sharply after the war, dental care had become a luxury for retirees, many retirees were forced to defer treatment or forgo necessary services, and some borrowed money or sold small assets to pay for care; the same report cited ILNA that insured patients still pay significant costs despite the legal promise of free Social Security treatment and may wait months for partial supplemental-insurance reimbursement.
claim.subject: Iranian retirees
claim.object: treatment because insurance and income do not cover health costs

evidence.summary: The report quoted Saeed Fatahi on drug/treatment costs, dental care as luxury, deferred care, borrowing/selling assets, and cited ILNA on out-of-pocket payments and delayed supplemental-insurance reimbursements.

information_depth.rationale: Named labor adviser, explicit mechanisms of deferred care, insurance gaps, and household coping behavior are reported.

claim.statement: On 30 April 2026, Iran International reported that war and economic crisis had deepened worker unemployment and health risk: it cited Etemad estimates of more than one million jobs lost and two million direct or indirect unemployed, Labor Minister Ahmad Meydari saying 147,000 people registered for unemployment insurance in two months, Ali Khodaei warning unemployment insurance covers less than half household costs, and construction-sector figures of 1.5-1.7 million workers with about half lacking Social Security coverage; the article linked this pressure to food insecurity and treatment deferral.
claim.subject: Iranian workers
claim.object: post-war unemployment, weak safety nets, and treatment/food insecurity

evidence.summary: The May Day article reported job-loss estimates, unemployment-insurance registrations, weak insurance replacement, construction-worker insurance gaps, and links to inability to pay food, rent, and treatment.

information_depth.rationale: Concrete job-loss, registration, sector, and health-risk figures are given, but some unemployment estimates are attributed indirectly.

question.text: Can treatment deferral and skipped essential medicines be quantified through pharmacy, hospital, insurer, or patient-association data rather than anecdotal reporting?
question.why_it_matters: Quantifying skipped care would show whether the health-access crack is isolated pain or a population-scale mortality risk.

relation.rationale: Direct worker/patient stories show how the documented medicine repricing appears as rationing, skipped medicines, and major out-of-pocket spending.
The ILNA cases include diabetes medicine and insulin scarcity, corroborating patient-level insulin access stress.
The official co-pay/coverage-disruption statement gives institutional context for rare-disease insurance warnings.
Both claims show retirees translating insurance failure and medicine/treatment costs into postponed care and protest pressure.
Unemployment, weak unemployment insurance, and lack of Social Security coverage compound the minimum-wage purchasing-power collapse.
The broader post-war unemployment article provides context for factory damage, layoffs, and wage-arrears evidence.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v8 — skipped care becomes worker survival signal
synthesis.summary: The eighth pass moves the health-access thread from institutional warning to lived triage. Direct ILNA reporting has workers and retirees naming exact medicines, cities, incomes, rent, and coping behavior: metformin roughly tripled, insulin is hard to find, a Tehran service worker paid 13M toman upfront for medicine against a 20M salary and 10M rent, a Rasht heart patient cannot afford Plavix and stretches specialist visits, and a Sanandaj teacher with cancer says insurance covers only about 10% of tests. This is reinforced by an Apr 19 retiree-care report: dental care is now described as a luxury, retirees defer treatment or skip services, and supplemental insurance reimbursement can be delayed for months. The state has noticed the pressure: ILNA quoted parliament's health-commission spokesman acknowledging drug price and patient co-pay disruption from coordination failures, even while claiming fixes. On the labor side, the May Day unemployment article adds the safety-net context: over 1M jobs estimated lost, 147k unemployment-insurance registrations in two months, and many construction workers uninsured. Net: the crack is now treatment triage under wage collapse, not just medicine inflation.
synthesis.limitations: The strongest skipped-care evidence is still qualitative, based on direct cases and named institutional warnings rather than population-scale pharmacy or insurer data. The parliamentary statement claims fixes and high hard-to-treat drug coverage, but that claim is not independently verified. xPool May Day results did not add reliable inside-Iran protest evidence in this pass.

information_depth.rationale: Direct ILNA patient narratives, named labor-adviser warning, official parliamentary statement, and May Day unemployment data converge on treatment triage under wage collapse.

change.reason: v8 adds direct patient/worker treatment-triage evidence, official drug co-pay disruption acknowledgement, retiree treatment deferral, and May Day unemployment/safety-net context.

Leader vows to defeat enemy in economic, cultural wars following Iran's victory on battlefield

claim.statement: On 1 May 2026, the official Khamenei.ir site published a Labor Day / Teacher Day message signed by Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei and state media presented him as the Leader issuing it; Mehr previewed the message from 'Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei, Leader of the Islamic Revolution,' and PressTV identified him in English as 'Leader of Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei.' This is a high-confidence official public leadership signal, but it does not by itself prove that he personally controls all war decisions.
claim.subject: Mojtaba Khamenei
claim.object: Leader issuing Labor Day and Teacher Day message

evidence.summary: Official Khamenei.ir page dated 1405/02/11 published the message and signed it Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei.
Mehr previewed the forthcoming message from Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei as Leader of the Islamic Revolution.
PressTV identified him in English as Leader of the Islamic Revolution and summarized the same Labor/Teacher Day message.

information_depth.rationale: The signal is recorded on the official Khamenei site and amplified by Persian and English state media on the same date.

assessment.uncertainty: This proves official public presentation and narrative control, not the full internal command structure.

claim.statement: In the 1 May 2026 Labor Day / Teacher Day message, Mojtaba Khamenei framed teachers as a core link in the cultural battle and workers as core elements in the economic battle after military victory; he said verbal praise was insufficient, called for stronger family-school interaction, prioritizing domestic goods, avoiding layoffs where possible, and government support for employers that keep workers.
claim.subject: Mojtaba Khamenei
claim.object: workers and teachers as economic-cultural war backbone

evidence.summary: The official message explicitly describes teachers as central to cultural battle, workers as central to economic battle, and calls for domestic-goods preference and avoiding layoffs.
PressTV's English summary repeats the economic/cultural war frame and the appeals for practical support, domestic goods, and avoiding layoffs.

information_depth.rationale: The claim summarizes the official text and state-media amplification rather than inferring hidden intent.

assessment.uncertainty: The message gives regime framing; it does not measure whether workers, teachers, employers, or families accept it.

relation.rationale: A named official message is directly relevant to whether Mojtaba is exercising visible authority or only serving as nominal cover.
The official message supports the regime narrative that Mojtaba is active, while still leaving health and actual command authority unresolved.
The official message counters reports of total absence or incapacity, but it is not a physical public appearance and could be managed messaging.
The official appeal to workers and teachers lands against direct evidence that workers, retirees, and teachers are already triaging medicine and care.
The message's economic-war framing targets the same labor base whose dollar-denominated minimum wage has fallen sharply.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v9 — Mojtaba surfaces as labor-war narrator
synthesis.summary: The ninth pass adds a current official leadership signal to v8's worker-health picture. On 1 May, Khamenei.ir, Mehr, and PressTV publicly presented Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei as the leader issuing the Labor Day / Teacher Day message. This does not prove he personally controls the IRGC or every war decision, but it narrows the open succession question: the regime is confident enough to put his signature and title on a public message to two sensitive social blocs. The content matters because workers and teachers were cast as the backbone of economic and cultural jihad after military victory, with appeals to buy domestic goods, avoid layoffs, deepen family-school interaction, and support employers that keep workers. That official mobilization language lands against the lived evidence already recorded: worker and retiree medicine triage, falling dollar-denominated minimum wage, unemployment risk, delayed insurance reimbursement, and teachers/retirees among the protesting or financially squeezed groups. Open-web May Day protest evidence in this pass was mostly old 1404 hits or low-confidence opposition-network social claims, so it is excluded from the core record. Net: the regime is layering succession projection and war-economy rhetoric over worker/teacher survival pressure.
synthesis.limitations: The Mojtaba signal is official public presentation, not independent proof of physical health, public appearance, or actual command authority. State-media wording should be treated as evidence of regime narrative and presentation, not as a neutral description of internal power. May Day protest material remains weak in this pass because many hits were 1404/2025 and xPool results were mostly uncorroborated opposition-network claims.

information_depth.rationale: Official and state-media sources establish the public presentation signal, while prior worker-health and wage claims ground the social-pressure interpretation.

change.reason: v9 adds the official Mojtaba Labor/Teacher Day leadership signal and economic-cultural war framing on top of v8's worker-health evidence.

claim.statement: On 23 April 2026, ILNA quoted Siaden Abhar steel workers saying about 250 contract workers remained employed but were owed Esfand 1404 and Farvardin 1405 wages, while about 15 reinstated workers were still owed Bahman wages; workers said last year's electricity-cut problem had caused several temporary shutdowns, production had restarted and accelerated from Farvardin, and their priorities were current monthly wages and preserving employment through higher production.

question.text: After 20 Ordibehesht 1405 (10 May 2026), do industrial power restrictions actually return, and do debt/transit-fee cutoffs create hidden shutdowns even if official rationing is delayed?
question.resolution_criteria: Post-10-May industrial power schedules; factory-level reports of outages; official notices from provincial power companies; worker reports of shutdowns or wage delays tied to electricity.
question.why_it_matters: Industrial electricity is a direct bridge between wartime infrastructure damage, unemployment, wage arrears, goods scarcity, and the regime's promise to avoid layoffs.

relation.rationale: Official delayed electricity restrictions and damaged dedicated power plants provide current context for factory shutdown and layoff pressure.
Fee/debt-related cutoffs show a second mechanism of industrial power loss even while official rationing is delayed.
Dena's rejected unemployment-insurance path and stop-start production corroborate wider post-war worker unemployment and weak safety-net pressure.
The Dena case shows the practical labor risk beneath Mojtaba's official call to avoid layoffs and support workers.
Siaden Abhar adds a factory-level wage-arrears and employment-preservation case to the broader unemployment/health-risk worker picture.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v10 — industrial power becomes employment pressure
synthesis.summary: The tenth pass adds an industrial-energy layer to the worker survival map. Officially, the Energy Ministry is delaying industrial electricity restrictions: Iran Online quoted the deputy energy minister saying industries can use full power until 20 Ordibehesht, after which continuation will be decided weekly, while factories with damaged dedicated power plants must repair/rebuild. But producer-side reporting already shows fragility beneath that promise: Jamaran/Vista says some production units have had power cut over unpaid 'transit' fees even after paying consumption charges, with one producer saying wartime conditions mean there is effectively no production or liquidity. ILNA then shows how this converts into labor exposure: in Fars, raw-material shortages tied to war damage and supply-chain disruption have pushed units into stop-start operation; Dena Tire's roughly 1,147 workers faced a rejected unemployment-insurance path for about 1,100 workers and were told to return. At Siaden Abhar steel, about 250 contract workers are still owed Esfand/Farvardin wages and are trying to preserve jobs through production after previous electricity-driven shutdowns. Net: Mojtaba's May Day appeal to avoid layoffs is colliding with power allocation, debt/fee enforcement, raw-material chokepoints, and wage arrears.
synthesis.limitations: Water-pressure results in this pass mostly duplicated existing Tehran-water rows and were not promoted. The transit-fee cutoff report lacks named firms or locations. The official industrial-power promise must be checked after 20 Ordibehesht with actual factory schedules, worker reports, and provincial power notices.

information_depth.rationale: The pass combines official energy timing, producer complaints, named labor-official reporting, and direct factory-worker reporting.

change.reason: v10 adds industrial electricity allocation, power/debt cutoff, raw-material stop-start operation, and factory-level wage/layoff exposure to v9's Mojtaba labor-war narrative.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v11 — campus life is still rationed
synthesis.summary: The eleventh pass adds a campus-life layer rather than a clean new protest wave. The reliable current signal is restriction and partial restoration. SNN says war/virtual-class conditions still leave dorm access banned or limited across major universities: Tehran, Alzahra, Shahid Beheshti, Iran University of Science and Technology, and Allameh are effectively closed or unavailable for ordinary dorming, while Sharif and Amirkabir allow narrow doctoral or graduate research cases. Net: campuses show the regime's post-war normalisation problem in miniature — knowledge work, housing, internet, and student politics are being selectively reopened while price anger now leaks even through regime-aligned student channels.
synthesis.limitations: Several apparent current student-protest hits were stale Esfand 1404 or older source pages republished by aggregators and were excluded. Khajeh Nasir welfare snippets look important but need a clean direct source/date before promotion. The Amirkabir Basij item is regime-aligned criticism, not a measure of broad student sentiment.

information_depth.rationale: The pass uses named universities, concrete access rules, international-internet details, and a dated institutional student statement while excluding stale protest hits.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v12 — campus rationing becomes campus discipline
synthesis.summary: The twelfth pass tightens the university picture. claim.statement: On 1 May 2026, official responses to Internet Pro showed ownership avoidance and internal pressure: a Ministry of Communications adviser said the ministry had issued no Internet Pro license and that the plan/proposal was not from the ministry or government, while the Article 90 Commission spokesman said people had the right to be upset about discrimination, white SIM cards as privileges for favorites were unacceptable, and the commission could seek a ministry report to resolve the discriminatory space.

question.text: Does official pressure over Internet Pro produce an actual rollback and restoration path for ordinary users, or only punish visible profiteers while preserving tiered access under a narrower crisis-service label?
question.resolution_criteria: Ministry directives, Article 90 follow-up, judiciary or regulator enforcement records, operator tariff changes, allocation lists, association follow-up statements, and measurable restoration of ordinary international internet access.

relation.rationale: The professional refusal/condemnation cluster directly answers the prior uncertainty about whether Internet Pro backlash was becoming organized.
This row is the strongest current evidence that the old Internet Pro backlash question is moving toward an organized refusal coalition.
The e-commerce association's statement frames Internet Pro as a rights, pricing, and technical-governance failure.
The association's duration figures and business-impact framing add institutional context to the national internet blackout claim.
Executive denial and parliamentary discrimination language show Internet Pro has become an official legitimacy liability, not only a public complaint.
The split between denial, investigation, and continued crisis-service framing is the key uncertainty for rollback versus containment.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v14 — Internet Pro refusal becomes cross-sector
synthesis.summary: The fourteenth pass moves Internet Pro from a student/citizen legitimacy problem into a cross-sector professional one. Persian near-primary reporting now shows Semnan lawyers, Isfahan lawyers, nurses, graphic designers, journalists, Sharif student bodies, and the Tehran E-Commerce Association either refusing special access, refusing collective applications, or condemning tiered internet as a public-rights violation. The most important update is not only that groups dislike the scheme; it is that they are refusing a scarce wartime advantage in public, using equality, legal rights, transparency, and civic solidarity language. The e-commerce association adds a harsher technical-economic indictment: more than 100 days of internet cuts in the past year, more than 60 continuous days during the recent war, security rationales that allegedly failed even on their own terms, and Internet Pro sold at at least five times the price. On 1 May, the state itself showed strain: a communications-ministry adviser denied ministry/government ownership or licensing, while the Article 90 Commission spokesman said people are entitled to be upset about discrimination and that white-SIM privileges for favorites are unacceptable. Net: tiered internet is now a regime-management failure with a visible refusal coalition, a digital-economy indictment, and officials trying to narrow or disown responsibility while preserving crisis-security language.
synthesis.limitations: This pass is strong on Persian, source-near public statements but still imperfect on original-web provenance: some association statements were recovered through Iranian media reproductions rather than association websites. The e-commerce duration and price claims are recorded as the association's public claims, not independently audited network measurements. Official distancing could mean real rollback pressure or only a narrowing of labels and enforcement against visible profiteers.

information_depth.rationale: The synthesis rests on multiple dated Persian sources, named professional bodies, and named/role-identified officials while explicitly separating direct statements from media reproductions.

change.reason: v14 adds a cross-sector Internet Pro refusal/condemnation cluster, the Tehran E-Commerce Association's technical-economic indictment, and official ownership-avoidance/investigation signals.

question.text: Do war-damaged pharmaceutical and distribution facilities plus FX/pricing delays turn today's price shock into measurable shortages over the next one to three months?
question.resolution_criteria: Food and Drug Organization shortage lists, pharmacy association reports, insulin and oncology drug availability, morphine/codeine/raw-material warnings, Titak stock data, patient-association statements, and evidence that damaged firms either did or did not return to stable production.

The official 44-company damage and raw-material constraints define the one-to-three-month shortage watch point.
The parliamentary session adds formal evidence that patient payment and pharmacy-search problems are visible to officials, but still not quantified at system level.
The official FX/pricing-delay mechanism directly supports prior patient reports of insulin access stress across cities.
The ILNA field report corroborates prior patient-level treatment triage and medicine-cost stress, with some official contestation over exact prices.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v16 - medicine becomes priced rationing
synthesis.summary: The sixteenth pass turns the medicine file from a price-shock story into a supply-chain and insurance story. Earlier KNB rows already captured the headline spike: about 5,000 drug items changing price, insulin and cancer drugs jumping, and patients deferring or rationing care. The new Persian/source-near evidence adds mechanism. Iran's Food and Drug Organization says 44 pharmaceutical, equipment, and distribution companies were damaged during Ramadan War, including full destruction of Tofigh Daru, with petrochemical/raw-material constraints, a roughly $5B annual medicine/equipment FX need, and insurance budgets up only 30%. The Health Ministry/Tehran MP session shows the system carrying 40,000 war wounded, damaged hospitals and health centers, killed health workers, drug distribution damage, and MPs openly reporting 20-30x medicine price complaints, pharmacy searches, and cash-before-service insurance failures. The Health Commission then identifies imported insulin as a live failure mode: domestic supply may exist, but foreign insulin imports/distribution are disrupted when FX allocation and price notices lag. xPool adds low-confidence street-level corroboration, including insulin self-rationing and pharmacy-search complaints. Net: the regime is preserving the form of medical continuity while pushing scarcity through price, insurance lag, local substitution, and delayed access - effectively priced rationing for patients who cannot wait.
synthesis.limitations: The strongest new rows are official or source-near Persian evidence, but official accounts may understate shortages and patient/social reports may overstate local prices or scarcity. xPool evidence is explicitly low-confidence. The decisive missing data remains pharmacy-level stock, insurer reimbursement timing, and patient-association counts for skipped doses or abandoned treatment.

information_depth.rationale: The synthesis combines official damage/FX mechanisms, parliamentary grievances, patient field reporting, prior price-spike rows, and low-confidence xPool corroboration while separating quantified official claims from anecdotal reports.

change.reason: v16 adds source-near Persian evidence that medicine access is moving from price shock into supply-chain, insurance, FX/pricing-delay, and patient self-rationing stress.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v17 - labor becomes the delayed fuse
synthesis.summary: The seventeenth pass shifts the labor file from visible protest counts toward a delayed-fuse model. The new Persian/source-near evidence does not yet show one unified nationwide labor command; xPool was noisy and did not add a strong direct in-country May Day protest-video cluster. What it does show is repeated sectoral pressure with shared mechanisms. Railway technical workers in Dorud and Andimeshk protested for a second day over arrears, the 1405 wage circular, benefits, and exclusion from wartime aid. Steel retirees in Isfahan and Tehran protested a nine-day supplementary-insurance gap because medicine, treatment, equipment, and hospital costs are now urgent. Energy-linked workers are squeezed from both sides: Ilam gas-refinery contractors demand return to work and arrears, while more than 700 Mahshahr petrochemical terminal workers report benefit cuts, shortened contracts, and lost transport/welfare support. Outside the protest scenes, ILNA reports at least 700 Borujerd textile layoffs, at least 2,000 Rasht layoffs across industrial/service units, and 90 Mokhmalkuh dam layoffs, with raw materials, finance, weak sales, and public-project funding as recurring causes. Retiree representatives now describe pensions, medicine, food, treatment, and Social Security debt as one combined survival issue. The state also appears to understand the risk: IRIB carried a May 1 Tabriz Friday-prayer sermon that acknowledged unmet worker/teacher livelihood demands while saying wartime law should govern and those creating public dissatisfaction should be dealt with severely. Net: labor has not become a coordinated national front in the evidence yet, but the same post-war channels - delayed pay, insurance gaps, benefit cuts, layoffs, and unemployment-insurance queues - are appearing across enough sectors to make labor a plausible delayed accelerant rather than a solved economic-management problem.
synthesis.limitations: Most of the strongest rows are source-near Persian labor reporting, but worker counts are often based on local sources rather than national audited statistics. Radio Farda and Daavtalab are useful aggregators but not primary for every sub-claim. xPool is explicitly low-confidence and noisy. The key missing evidence remains union/retiree coordination data, unemployment-insurance application totals, factory reopen/closure follow-through, and whether protests synchronize across sectors rather than repeating locally.

information_depth.rationale: The synthesis combines multiple ILNA source-near labor reports, one state-media security-framing source, one cross-sector aggregator, one labor-rights analysis, and a noisy xPool check while avoiding a stronger coordination claim than the evidence supports.

synthesis.title: Iran regime-stress map: 17-30 April 2026 (Persian-source-weighted)
synthesis.summary: Cracks visible across five reinforcing layers as of late Ordibehesht 1405. Layer 1 (currency / household pressure): the open-market dollar broke 180,000 toman on 29 April, a 120% rise from pre-12-day-war levels and a historic record low for the rial; BBC Persian and Iran International report households selling assets and buying on credit. Layer 2 (industrial collapse and labor unrest): Iran International reports only ~60 of 1,500 factories operating in the Tabriz Salimi estate; ~250 export/digital companies fully closed; HRANA/ILNA confirmed at least four labor protests on 29 April including steel pensioners in Esfahan and Tehran and railway workers in Dorud and Andimeshk; Tehran University staff struck 26 April; Eghtesad-e Irani describes a 'resignation domino' inside government and the head of the Plan & Budget Organization publicly apologized on 1 May for the 20% wage gap. Layer 3 (legitimacy and bazaar): on 27 April 2026 even state news agencies (ISNA/Fars/IRNA) acknowledged scattered protest gatherings inside Tehran's Grand Bazaar with chanting on Naser-Khosrow Street; Jahan-e Sanat reported partial bazaar closure on 29 April driven by exchange-rate anger. Layer 4 (regime cohesion): Reuters (28 April) and a NYT/Farnaz Fassihi report (relayed by Melliun and Straits Times) describe Mojtaba Khamenei as a 'figure of assent rather than command' while a 'board' of IRGC generals (Vahidi, Zolqadr, Rahim Safavi) makes operational calls; Radio Farda flags a Zolqadr/Jalili-vs-Qalibaf rift inside the SNSC; multiple Persian outlets describe a real Aref-Qaempanah dispute with Aref reportedly filing a resignation Pezeshkian declined to accept. Layer 5 (regime self-assessment): per Iran International (relayed by Jerusalem Post and JNS, 28 April), the SNSC itself was briefed that protests are 'inevitable,' that Iran's economy 'cannot withstand more than six to eight weeks' of continued US naval blockade, that ~2 million private-sector workers will lose jobs by end of spring, and that protests during talks could 'pose a real risk of the fall of the Islamic Republic.' What is NOT yet a crack: the visible Salmas / Langarud / Farahan night-marches are state-organized بیعت (allegiance) rallies for the new Supreme Leader, not anti-regime protests, and should not be confused with the labor/bazaar protest wave. Net read: the regime is under cumulative stress that even its own security apparatus describes in regime-collapse language; the missing ingredient versus 2022 (Mahsa) and December 2025 (Dey 1404) is a single politicized trigger event capable of bridging the still-sectoral labor/bazaar protests into a unified street movement.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v18 - food pressure reaches the calorie floor
synthesis.summary: The eighteenth pass moves the crack map from labor as delayed fuse into the bread and calorie layer. The strongest new signal is not a national bread riot; it is a management contradiction. Officials say no new flour or bread policy exists, bread-price increases are violations, and the state is still paying large bread subsidies, yet the guild side says sangak and barbari are not being sold at official rates, bakers are effectively taking about double, all sides are dissatisfied, and the decision is deferred to end-Khordad. That fits the older citizen layer: flour shortages, long bakery lines, barbari around 25,000 toman, and sangak around 35,000 in reports from 20 April. The food squeeze is already quantified: a standard four-person worker food basket was estimated at 25.159 million toman, or 85% of a married minimum worker household's 29.575 million toman income, after 68% average food-price growth over four months. The state is responding through kalabarg, not stability: Mehr/INN report triple-digit food inflation before war effects, a one-million-toman food-credit framework after 28,500-toman FX removal, and possible periodic increases from 15 Ordibehesht or Khordad based on food-basket and calorie scenarios. Official logistics reporting is also defensive: basic-goods routes have shifted from southern ports to northern ports and land borders, 3-6 month stock resilience is being built, and 50 thousand billion toman liquidity was announced for basic goods. The soft spot inside the reassurance is wheat procurement and farmer payment delays, plus a sugar report that says prices have not increased while expecting a mid-Ordibehesht correction. xPool is noisy and does not show a clean bakery-riot cluster, but it does show repeated social chatter about bread queues, kalabarg insufficiency, and basic-food price stress. Net: food has not yet become a unified street front in the evidence, but bread is now a live governance test where formal prices, actual prices, subsidies, and household calories no longer line up cleanly.
synthesis.limitations: State-linked supply and stock claims are useful because they reveal official management variables, but they may overstate resilience. Iran International citizen messages and xPool are noisy and should not be used as audited national statistics. The current evidence supports bread/food pressure and gray-market pricing, not yet a coordinated bread-riot or national rationing claim.

information_depth.rationale: The synthesis combines official/semi-official Persian reporting, existing citizen and price-table evidence, quantified worker food-basket estimates, and a low-confidence xPool social check while avoiding a riot claim.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v19 - executions become wartime governance
synthesis.summary: The nineteenth pass hardens the repression layer. The execution story is no longer just scattered named cases; it is becoming wartime governance. UN/OHCHR and CHRI now converge on a rapid post-war political-execution campaign: at least 21-22 political executions in the recent post-war window, more than 4,000 national-security arrests, ten January 2026 protesters among the executed, and dozens more facing death sentences or capital charges, including women and 17-year-olds. The Sasan Azadvar case shows the mechanism: state media recodes a 21-year-old Dey protest detainee into a Mossad/US-Israel wartime enemy actor, while HRANA/BBC describe a rushed, legally contested moharebeh case built around stones/clubs, forced-confession concerns, limited legal time, and security-restricted burial. The lane is broader than protesters: BBC/Euronews/RFI show an MEK/old-opposition execution lane, with Soltanali Shirzadi executed on 23 April and multiple alleged MEK-linked prisoners executed since the war began. Prison resistance persists but is under pressure: week 118 of No to Executions Tuesdays is reported across 56 facilities, while Evin women prisoners were reportedly threatened with solitary and phone cutoffs for participation. The next near-term danger cluster is Orumiyeh, where KHRN says Nasser Bakerzadeh, Yaghoub Karimpour, and Mehrab Abdollahzadeh were moved to unknown locations after Bakerzadeh's death sentence was confirmed for a third time. xPool shows heavy anti-execution chatter and named-case amplification, but not a clean in-country street cluster. Net: executions look less like routine repression and more like the regime's chosen bridge between war-security narrative, deterrence, and information control. Whether this suppresses action or makes martyrs is now a central crack question.
synthesis.limitations: Counts use different windows and source methods, so 21 vs 22 should be treated as convergent scale, not exact harmonized accounting. NCRI/IranHRS/KHRN are advocacy or opposition-adjacent sources and need follow-up, but the UN/CHRI/BBC/IRIB anchors are strong enough to treat execution acceleration and official enemy-framing as high-confidence. The xPool sample is useful as reaction evidence only; blackout conditions likely suppress in-country signal.

information_depth.rationale: This synthesis combines direct state media, Persian international reporting, UN/OHCHR reporting, rights-group tallies, Kurdish rights reporting, prison-campaign reporting, and a bounded xPool social sample.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v20 - price discovery becomes a security problem
synthesis.summary: The twentieth pass shifts back to the economic street layer. The strongest new pattern is not yet a clean nationwide Bazaar strike; it is that normal price discovery has become a security problem. Official sources and state-aligned outlets describe a 17-point FX-control package, second-hall intervention, FX funds, currency Murabaha tools, increased import allocations, and informal-market intervention, but by 30 April the free dollar was still around 177k-180k toman while the controlled second-hall dollar was near 140k-141.5k. Fararu/Donyaye Eqtesad shows the physical market repricing in real time: cash dollar 171k to 178k and back toward 172k, Tether 165k to 179.5k, 18k gold above 20m toman, and the new coin around 202.67m even as global gold fell. IranWire adds the governance reaction: after a 157k to 182k dollar move in 48 hours, forces reportedly told FX shops to close and turn off boards, prevented Aladdin merchants from standing together, and pushed closed-shop owners to leave. The mobile market itself is a livelihood signal, with shortage and price reports turning phones and internet access into luxury goods. The odd Manouchehri/Ferdowsi Iran-check premium shows another stress: even physical rial cash can acquire a rent under crisis conditions. Formal financial markets are also being managed by suspension, with share trading halted through 14 Ordibehesht while selected low-risk instruments continue. xPool amplifies Ferdowsi/Aladdin/security/strike rumors and expectations for a Saturday strike, but does not confirm a sustained post-April-29 Bazaar action. Net: the crack is forced non-market silence. The regime can still cap visible collective action, but it is doing so by suppressing quotes, closing venues, policing ordinary merchant clustering, and freezing parts of the capital market, all while the underlying price pressure keeps leaking through.
synthesis.limitations: IranWire's security details are witness-style and medium-confidence under blackout conditions. Vista mirrors provide only partial access to some state-aligned FX-control articles, so policy-source depth should be improved with direct CBI/IRNA/Tasnim originals if accessible. xPool is useful for chatter and rumor topology only. The key unresolved item is whether 2-4 May produces verified Bazaar or mobile-market strike activity rather than rumor and forced quiet.

information_depth.rationale: The pass combines domestic Persian market reporting, state-aligned policy reporting, field-style IranWire reporting, capital-market closure reporting, an older field report on cash distortions, and a bounded xPool social sample.

synthesis.summary: The May 2 follow-up weakens the narrow hypothesis of a verified Saturday Bazaar/Ferdowsi/Aladdin strike, but strengthens the broader forced-quiet hypothesis. Exa Persian searches and the xPool latest-timeline query found anticipation and rumor, not source-near confirmation of a sustained May 2 strike. Price pressure has not disappeared: Eghtesad Moaser put the free dollar at 177,910 toman on May 1, up 14% in a week and 117% in a year, while Safhe Eghtesad/Vista put the commercial exchange-center dollar at 141,531 toman as import/trade demand returned. The governance reaction is more revealing than the absence of a confirmed strike. SNN's May 1 judiciary article frames market disruption as a security/legal problem, invokes cooperation with supervisory, intelligence, and security bodies, and orders prosecutor-led market-supervision working groups with ministries, Tazirat, and guilds. Iran International and IranWire also report a serious, still-contested Starlink-linked death of Hossam Aladdin, a relative of the Aladdin mall owner; that claim needs corroboration, but it fits the wider pattern of internet and market control converging. Net: the regime may be preventing visible merchant collective action, but only by moving price discovery, communications tools, guild behavior, and ordinary market clustering into the security domain.
synthesis.limitations: This is a bounded May 2 search pass, not proof that no strike occurred. The xPool sample is algorithmic and sparse. The Hossam Aladdin/Starlink death reporting is important but contested, and IranWire's article contains an impossible burial-date detail. Follow-up should prioritize May 2-4 source-near Bazaar/Aladdin/Ferdowsi reports and any official/guild statements about reopening or enforcement.

information_depth.rationale: The pass combines source-near search notes, a bounded xPool query, domestic market-price reporting, a state-aligned judiciary signal, and two rights/repression reports, while explicitly preserving uncertainty around negative strike evidence and the Aladdin report.

relation.rationale: The May 2 follow-up directly updates the open question about whether Aladdin/Ferdowsi Saturday strike rumors become verifiable action or containment.
The judiciary's market-supervision order is a concrete state-containment mechanism to test against May 2-4 market behavior.
Both claims connect Aladdin/mobile-market pressure with security handling of communications and market-adjacent networks, though the Hossam Aladdin report remains contested.

change.reason: v21 adds the May 2 verification pass, distinguishing unconfirmed strike rumors from stronger evidence of forced quiet, continued currency pressure, and security/judicial containment.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v22 - the communications workaround is criminalized
synthesis.summary: The v22 pass shows communications control becoming one of the regime's most concrete pressure points. After more than two months of disrupted international internet, the workaround itself is being turned into a security offense. ANA's report on a Tehran judiciary-prevention SMS says the whole Starlink chain - import, supply, distribution, carrying, storage, sale, installation, operation, and use - is forbidden and punishable. State-aligned reporting then shows that frame in practice: Sirik authorities arrested and jailed two people after a Starlink shipment seizure; Shemiranat/Lavasanat officials reported 10 devices seized in villas and said dealers and support networks would be pursued; Tehran police-linked reports described an arrest at a Fereshteh commercial unit, three northwest Tehran guild units sealed, and a Yusefabad apartment framed as a Starlink-equipped spy base. A Yazd police item, still needing direct-source upgrade, adds financial coercion with 61 suspect-linked bank accounts reportedly frozen. xPool shows the social layer: the May 1 sample is dominated by Starlink/Hossam Aladdin discourse, mixing outrage, fear, Internet Pro resentment, and regime/skeptical narratives. The crack is that the state needs the internet restricted, but households, traders, businesses, and information networks need outside connectivity; the workaround for that need is now being criminalized across the user, business, supply-chain, banking, and residential layers.
synthesis.limitations: Most enforcement details are state or state-aligned police/judiciary claims; they are strong evidence for the official crackdown and framing, not independent proof of espionage. The Yazd account-freeze item is from Vista aggregation and should be upgraded with direct Fars/police text. xPool provides discourse topology, not representative polling or verification.

information_depth.rationale: The pass combines domestic legal reporting, multiple Persian enforcement reports, a provincial judicial source, internet-blackout reporting, and a bounded xPool discourse sample.

relation.rationale: Full-chain Starlink criminalization is the coercive mirror image of Internet Pro/tiered-internet privilege and legitimacy backlash.
The xPool discourse sample shows how the contested Hossam Aladdin report circulated and split into outrage, fear, and counter-narratives.
The prolonged blackout explains why Starlink and privileged access become politically salient workarounds before being criminalized.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v23 - May Day exposes managed grievance
synthesis.summary: The May Day / Teacher Day pass does not show a verified nationwide labor strike, but it does show the regime's labor problem in a clear form. Official and semi-official channels can still contain the day inside ritual: the House Worker May Day resolution praises wartime labor and packages demands through recognized bodies, while SNN's Teacher Day item turns teachers into allegiance/resistance actors around Mojtaba Khamenei. But the content of the managed channels is still hard-edged: Social Security needs urgent support, inspection and job security must improve, retirees cannot cover living/treatment/housing costs, and Fars alone has about 15k unemployment-insurance recipients costing roughly 100b toman per month. ILNA's West Azerbaijan workers say they need security and real support instead of ceremonial greetings after post-war factory closures and layoffs. HRANA's annual review supplies the structural backdrop: thousands of worker casualties, hundreds of gatherings and strikes, documented arrests and punishments, and lower reported strike/gathering numbers amid repression and disorganization. xPool confirms the social layer is politically charged but diffuse: 87 labor hits and 11 teacher hits in a 100-item sample, without a clean national coordination signal. Net: the crack is not yet a May Day general strike; it is that even loyal and managed labor/teacher rituals are forced to speak the language of survival, job security, healthcare, unpaid benefits, and inflation.
synthesis.limitations: This pass is strong for grievance taxonomy and May Day framing, but weak for offline coordination. The xPool sample is not representative, and official/House Worker sources describe managed channels rather than independent labor organizing. Follow-up should check May 2-7 for repeat worker/retiree/teacher actions after the ceremony window closes.

information_depth.rationale: The pass combines domestic labor reporting, HRANA annual statistics, state-aligned Teacher Day framing, existing KNB protest rows, and a bounded xPool discourse sample.

relation.rationale: The annual strike/gathering/repression counts update the question of whether labor protests are coalescing or remaining sectoral/local.
The House Worker demand package shows labor grievances being kept in a lawful/managed frame for now.
The social sample supports dispersed grievance rather than clear coordination, but follow-up is required.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v24 - rationing without saying rationing
synthesis.summary: The service-stress layer is now visible in the regime's own vocabulary. Tehran's water system is not being described as formally rationed, but officials and Persian reports say pressure is reduced from midnight to morning to lower leakage and refill reservoirs; local reports put Tehran dams at 9 percent full with Taleghan and 3 percent without, while Karaj dam had only about a two-week margin for Tehran drinking water. Mashhad shows the same denial structure: four drinking-water dams were reported 94 percent empty while officials still said there was no rationing plan. Electricity has a parallel May 10 cliff: industries get full power only until 20 Ordibehesht, then weekly decisions by temperature, consumption, and production, while semi-official commentary warns industrial cutoffs threaten employment and national security. The power grid is also being framed as stable despite tens of thousands of billions of tomans in war damage and thousands of damaged network points, with officials asking households to save before a hot, dry summer. xPool does not yet show a broad social wave around services; it mostly adds scattered ground texture and noise. Net: the crack is not mass service unrest yet, but euphemistic rationing and official consumption discipline moving into ordinary water and power use.
synthesis.limitations: This pass is strong for official and Persian media admissions around pressure management, dam stress, and post-May-10 industrial-power risk. It is weaker for direct lived-service mapping: xPool produced only scattered anecdotes, and several water figures came through Vista aggregations rather than direct water-company pages. Follow-up should revisit May 10 industrial electricity, direct Tehran/Mashhad pressure schedules, and neighborhood-level reports of daytime water cutoffs.

information_depth.rationale: The pass combines official statements, Persian local reporting, existing KNB water/electricity questions, and a bounded social-media noise check.

relation.rationale: The pressure-management pattern is the current bridge between official no-rationing language and household rationing risk.
The 9 percent / 3 percent dam figures and Karaj two-week margin materially update the Day Zero question.
Mashhad shows the same low-storage/no-rationing official posture that Tehran had before pressure controls intensified.
The May 10 full-power cutoff date directly defines the next verification window for industrial restrictions.
The social sample supplies bounded negative evidence: scattered anecdotes but no broad coordinated service-disruption wave yet.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v27 - Internet Pro becomes controlled selective access
synthesis.summary: The twenty-seventh pass answers the v14 Internet Pro rollback question in the direction of containment, not restoration. The newer official architecture is now clearer: Reza Alizadeh's SNSC account puts the scope and limits of international-internet access under security bodies, starts access with business-card holders and production/industry/commerce organizations, and obligates the three mobile operators to implement. The Government spokesperson then frames Internet Pro as an SNSC-approved crisis-business continuity measure and says internet status will change only when responsible bodies declare normal conditions, without giving a date or public restoration mechanism. The Communications Ministry adviser denial is therefore not a clean rollback; it is an ownership and abuse-management move. He says the Ministry issued no license and the scheme was not a Ministry/Government plan, while regulator/judiciary follow-up targets bad implementation and public or black-market sale. xPool matches that reading: visible Persian discourse clusters around license, violations, judiciary, MCI, black-market activation, boycott calls, and business-continuity defenses, not measurable restoration of ordinary internet. Net: the crack is not that censorship collapsed; it is that economic need forces exceptions, the exception market becomes visibly classed and corrupt, and the state has to discipline the exception while preserving security-controlled selective access.
synthesis.limitations: This pass is strong on official architecture and discourse topology but still lacks the decisive artifacts: the SNSC resolution text, regulator tariff files, operator contracts, allocation lists, enforcement outcomes, and direct network measurements showing whether ordinary international internet is restored or remains blocked. xPool evidence is amplification and framing evidence only.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v28 - unemployment becomes an administrative containment problem
synthesis.summary: The twenty-eighth pass turns the labor layer from May Day grievance into a concrete post-war employment-containment file. The strongest official number is no longer vague: Labor Minister Ahmad Meydari says about 150,000 people have registered for unemployment insurance after the 40-day war. But the number is also incomplete by design, because damaged large units such as steel and petrochemical sites may still be paying wages and not sending workers to Labor offices. State support architecture is expanding around that risk: more than 43,000 damaged businesses entering support registration, more than 3,000 damaged industrial units with packages by damage level, 44-million-toman per-worker SME loans in the search record, and a May 1 parliamentary line that no worker should be fired in these conditions. Electricity policy is now part of the same containment logic: full industrial power is promised until 20 Ordibehesht and later restrictions are advertised as support for production continuity, but weekly decisions and damaged captive-power plants keep the summer risk live. xPool shows the social layer is harsher than the administrative layer: discourse is dominated by layoff, firing, worker, war, blackout, steel, and petrochemical language, with official denial of Steel Mobarakeh layoffs competing against worker-side anger about internet and war-driven business collapse. Net: the regime has not lost the labor file, but it is trying to prevent a production shock from becoming a worker street shock through payroll continuation, insurance queues, loans, anti-layoff messaging, patriotic consumption appeals, and industrial-power promises.
synthesis.limitations: The official numbers are administrative and may undercount informal, contract, platform, and internet-dependent workers. The larger 1-2 million job-loss estimate needs direct corroboration before being treated as more than a reported estimate. xPool is discourse evidence only. The decisive follow-up is payment reality: who actually receives wages, unemployment insurance, loans, and electricity continuity between 10 and 20 Ordibehesht.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v41 - Measurements confirm selective access, not restoration
synthesis.summary: The forty-first pass closes the measurement gap left by v40. The apparent conflict between '1-3%' and 'above 10%' connectivity is not a real contradiction. IODA says active probing fell to about 3% on February 28 and had not recovered by April 27; CHN/KhabarOnline citing NetBlocks puts the May 1/day-63 broad connectivity level at 1-2%; and Safhe Eghtesad/CITNA says estimates above 10% mainly reflect non-public routes such as Internet Pro, special access, organizational access, and specific network paths. Internet Society Pulse classifies the shutdown as ongoing and describes recovery as patchy, filtered, sector-specific, fixed-IP/allowlist-based, and not open consumer restoration. AP adds the social/economic cost: 90m people largely cut off from the global web, $30-40m in direct daily losses, possible indirect losses twice that, and about 10m jobs tied to internet connectivity, while white SIMs and limited professional access remain. Net: the measurement layer supports the same diagnosis as the policy layer: the regime has not restored ordinary public internet; it has preserved a managed exception system and allowed special-path recovery to masquerade as improvement.
synthesis.limitations: Direct May 1 NetBlocks data was found via syndications/search excerpts rather than a standalone crawled NetBlocks post. Direct OONI, Cloudflare Radar, Kentik, operator-level, and user-measurement dashboards would further strengthen granularity. Treat the 10%+ estimate as a near-primary Persian technical claim about special access, not a public-connectivity baseline.

information_depth.rationale: The synthesis combines measurement-platform interpretation, current NetBlocks-citing reporting, a Persian technical reconciliation of special-path access, AP field reporting, and v40 policy/discourse rows.

relation.rationale: The claim directly answers the rollback/restoration question using independent measurement and near-measurement evidence.
The Pulse record frames the shutdown as ongoing and the recovery as selective/managed rather than public rollback.
The shutdown's business-collapse and job-dependency numbers are a likely driver of delayed layoffs and labor stress.
The same selective-access architecture affects education and campus life through unstable/filtered connectivity.

change.reason: v41 adds independent network-measurement evidence showing that Internet Pro/special-path recovery is not ordinary public restoration.

question.text: Can source-near labor-market records confirm the scale of digital-economy job loss from the blackout, especially unemployment-insurance registrations, IranTalent/LinkedIn hiring data, firm layoff notices, or union member surveys?

question.resolution_criteria: Find direct datasets, official labor-office filings, named firm notices, IranTalent/LinkedIn metrics, or union survey methodology that can quantify digital-economy layoffs separately from broader war and inflation shocks.

synthesis.title: Cracks in the Islamic Republic, v42 - The blackout becomes a labor-market shock
synthesis.summary: The forty-second pass reframes the shutdown as an employment shock rather than only a connectivity/control story. v41 showed that 'Internet Pro' and special access are not public restoration. v42 shows what that managed exception system is doing to the workforce: the flagship DigiKala case is now bounded at about 200 layoffs / 3%; a Nasr-linked online-services report says some IoT/services firms have cut 30-50% of staff and may need more than a year to recover; Persian union/business reporting puts large-firm sales losses around 50-80%, Instagram-shop livelihood exposure in the millions, and customer/marketing access as the unsolved problem even when firms receive limited connectivity; AP and Iran International field reporting show concrete worker paths from remote-work loss to layoffs, business closure, street vending, and migration pressure; and a 180-item xPool sample shows blackout-linked job-loss language is socially live, though noisy. Net: the regime's internet policy is no longer only producing anger about unequal access. It is now visibly turning digital livelihoods into layoffs, informal work, and exit pressure, which connects the internet crack to the broader delayed labor-unrest question.
synthesis.limitations: Exact national job-loss totals remain unresolved. Some figures count exposed livelihoods, some count sales losses, some count layoffs, and some are social/discourse claims. DigiKala's layoff cause is mixed and cannot be reduced to a blackout-only causal claim. The Net-Mag/IranTalent 57% hiring-demand figure is a useful lead but low confidence until the underlying dataset or Roomit article is found.

information_depth.rationale: The synthesis combines field reporting, company-confirmed layoff numbers, sector-official claims, business-union estimates, and an archived social sample, while keeping exact job-count uncertainty explicit.

relation.rationale: A 30-50% layoff range in some online-services firms is direct evidence for the delayed labor-protest and unemployment-pressure question.
Field reports connect the blackout to worker-level outcomes: job loss, street vending, small-business closure, and migration pressure.
The social sample shows blackout/job-loss anger escaping narrow professional complaint language and attaching to broader anti-regime labor-economic grievance.

change.reason: v42 preserves v41's measurement finding and adds evidence that the managed blackout is now producing visible digital-economy layoffs, income collapse, and migration pressure.

synthesis.title: Cracks at depth, 17 Apr – 1 May 2026 — apex, axis, alloy
synthesis.summary: Three deeper-cut fissures complete the picture. APEX (the Khamenei family + aghazadeh): a Khamenei niece was arrested on 24 Apr after publicly condemning the regime, while Dominica revoked the Caribbean citizenship of a second Shamkhani-family member on 18 Apr — closing the elite hedging hatch and signalling a visible split inside the apex itself. AXIS (the proxy and external-backer architecture): Lebanese press (Lebanon24, Elsiyasa) on 29 Apr reported that Iran is reducing its support for Hezbollah, while Bloomberg (22 Apr) and RFE/RL (17 Apr) document that Xi Jinping's support has explicit limits — Iran's strategic-depth and external-rescue scenarios are simultaneously cratering. ALLOY (legitimacy in the cultural surface): an organised diaspora movement on 30 Apr–1 May demanded that FIFA ban Iran from the 2026 World Cup ('they are not representing Iran'); a global movement campaigned to halt Toomaj Salehi's execution; the Supreme Court confirmed the Abbasi family death sentences on 27 Apr; healthcare is fragile per MSF on top of 50 reported damaged hospitals; and gold/currency are in 'explosive surge' alongside US-tracked capital flight. The Zayandeh-Rud release is being pushed to late Ordibehesht — re-arming the Isfahan-farmer flashpoint at the worst possible moment. Read together with the prior 19 cracks in iran-cracks/ and iran-margins/, the regime's apex, axis, and alloy are degrading in lockstep — i.e., the failure modes are no longer single-domain.
synthesis.limitations: The Khamenei-niece arrest rests on a single second-tier wire; verify before high-confidence use. Lebanon24/Elsiyasa Hezbollah pieces are directionally clear but qualitatively-framed; magnitude unproven. JaFaJ capital-flight claim is low-tier and should be re-anchored to a Treasury OFAC release before promotion above 'medium' confidence.

synthesis.title: Cracks at the margins, 17 Apr – 1 May 2026 — bazaar, Bahá'ís, conscripts, oil, IRIB, Afghans
synthesis.summary: Pulling on the under-covered seams: (a) Tehran Bazaar — historically the single most loaded commercial-class signal in Iranian regime collapse — shut down nationwide on 29 Apr in protest of the rial collapse, after merchant gatherings on 20 and 27 Apr (ISNA/Fars/IRNA on the regime side, Jahan-Sanat on the dissent side). (b) Bahá'í minority pressure intensified: the Universal House of Justice publicly named two Bahá'í cousins, Peyvand and Borna Naimi, as facing execution; three Bahá'í women jailed in Kerman; sustained detentions in Mashhad, Shiraz, Isfahan. (c) Conscription strain visible in policy: on 28 Apr the regime announced fresh fines for absent or runaway conscripts — a tightening rarely reached for unless desertion is real. (d) Oil dark-fleet under sustained pressure: 24 Apr Treasury sanctions on ~20 companies and 19 ships including Hengli (Dalian); 25 Apr CENTCOM interception of M/V Sevan; tankers systematically going dark per Bloomberg, clustering shy of the blockade line off Chabahar. (e) IRIB compromise public: an IRIB-affiliated outlet acknowledged a 'third American-Zionist attack' on state TV on 27 Apr; France 24 (mirrored) reports state TV was hijacked to broadcast a Reza Pahlavi speech ~29 Apr — likely Predatory Sparrow. (f) Afghan migrants as the regime's pressure-release valve: per the UN, >120,000 deported in Q1 2026, with single-day expulsions of 6,000–7,000 reported on 18-19 Apr — classic crisis scapegoating. (g) Hijab posture re-tightened: IRGC deputy commander warned women on 22 Apr that hijab is 'God's own command'; Iran International framed the post-war regime as 'returning to the 60s' on gender. (h) A second elite-defection signal: a senior reformist publicly called for 'courage in flexibility, not endless confrontation' on 21 Apr — paralleling Rouhani's 'great change'. (i) Friday-prayer optics: regime mouthpiece SNN aired an unusually loud 1 May line about 'not emptying the streets' — its emphasis itself diagnostic. Together these sit underneath the headline cracks (command vacuum, currency collapse, labour, infrastructure, clergy defection, students, prisons, pharma, cyber, Kurdistan) — i.e., the regime's external valves (oil, refugees, broadcasting) and its internal coercion levers (Bahá'í minority, hijab, conscripts) are simultaneously stressed, while the bazaar is starting to blink red.
synthesis.limitations: Two-week window. Persian on-the-ground signal is dampened by the national internet blackout; reliance on diaspora outlets (Iran International, Hengaw, Kayhan London) and regime-side counter-mouthpieces (Jam-e Jam, SNN, Sharq Daily) is mitigated by recording each side's framing alongside the other. Bazaar closure scope (Tehran-only vs. multi-city) and IRIB-hijack provenance (Predatory Sparrow attribution) carry the largest residual uncertainty.

relation.rationale: Internal-family arrest amid external-proxy retreat illustrates the regime simultaneously losing legitimacy at the apex and abandoning frontier commitments.
Loss of Shamkhani Caribbean passport is the most concrete expression of the broader aghazadeh-visibility trend.
With Chinese backing capped, Iran has fewer external resources to underwrite Hezbollah; both sit on the regime's external-rescue collapse.
MSF independent assessment corroborates regime-side hospital-damage scale.
Gold/currency surge and tracked capital flight describe two faces of the same flight-to-safety dynamic.
Tehran Bazaar shutdown is downstream of currency collapse, which is downstream of oil-export squeeze (tankers going dark to evade blockade caps revenue).
IRGC deputy's official threat instantiates the analytical claim that the regime is reverting to 1980s-style enforcement.
Predatory-Sparrow IRIB hijack is one of the attacks the regime acknowledged on 27 April.
Sevan interception followed directly from prior-day Treasury sanctions designating that vessel.

claim.statement: IranTalent-linked reporting in February-April 2026 shows a severe demand-side hiring freeze after the internet cutoff: TejaratNews/Zoomit quoted IranTalent CEO Asiyeh Hatami saying hiring demand fell 57% after internet disruptions, compared with 35% during the 12-day war, and that SMEs saw a 74% demand drop in the first three weeks of the international-internet cutoff; Zoomit later reported IranTalent data showing a 78% year-over-year drop in spring job opportunities for specialists and educated workers, from an earlier comparable average of about 65k opportunities per month to roughly four of five opportunities absent.

claim.object: large hiring-demand and job-opportunity collapse after internet disruptions

evidence.summary: TejaratNews/Zoomit quotes IranTalent CEO Asiyeh Hatami on 57% overall hiring-demand decline, 74% SME decline, 35% war-period comparison, hiring freezes at large companies, and internet businesses hit hardest.
Zoomit reports IranTalent data that spring specialist/educated-worker opportunities fell 78% year-over-year, from a comparable prior-year average near 65k opportunities/month.
The notes distinguish hiring demand and job-opportunity metrics from direct unemployment counts.
